payload.rationale: Without current data for September 2026, we rely on macroeconomic projections from 2023/2024. The Federal Reserve was expected to execute a rate-cutting cycle through 2024 and 2025, bringing the federal funds rate down to a neutral level of around 3-4%. Historically, a 3-4% Fed funds rate corresponds to a 30-year fixed mortgage rate of roughly 5-6.5%. For the rate to remain above 7.01% by September 2026, inflation would likely have needed to rebound or remain stubbornly high, forcing the Fed to maintain restrictive policy. While possible, this is not the baseline consensus. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is if the rate-cutting cycle brought mortgage rates well below 6%, making a rate above 7.01% highly improbable. The strongest reason it could be too low is if a second wave of inflation or massive Treasury issuance pushed long-term yields and mortgage rates back above 7%.
limitations: No data available from 2024 to September 2026.
Complete reliance on outdated macroeconomic projections.
